text: The land had emptied.
The lakefront that became Hyde Park stayed empty a while longer.
The same sand that turned the portage into a crossing made this ground poor for crops.
Nathan Watson learned that the hard way.
He tried to farm a stretch near the Chicago-to-Detroit wagon road,
around what is now 53rd Street and Lake Park.
That road was not new.
It followed the old Sauk Trail,
the Native footpath that ran from the Mississippi at Rock Island east to the Detroit River,
the same kind of trail the Potawatomi had walked for generations before a surveyor ever touched it.
Watson dreamed of an orchard.
The sand beat him.
So he turned his place into a tavern and fed the travelers passing through.
When he died, his widow, Electa Watson, ran it as a boarding house and farm,
the only real structure for miles along that shore.
The same country still surrounded it.
Sand ridges with bur oaks, swales of wildflowers, prairie to the horizon.
A young lawyer rode straight into that country in 1853.
Paul Cornell came six miles south from the city most mornings just to buy a
glass of buttermilk from Electa Watson at the tavern.
That August he gambled.
He bought three hundred acres of lakefront that no one else wanted and sank nearly
everything he had into the sand.
He named the place Hyde Park, after the London park.
Within a few years he deeded sixty of those acres to the Illinois Central Railroad
and won a depot at 53rd Street and a promise of daily trains to the
city.
The grocery clerks, the elevated trains, the university all lay decades off.
The bur oaks and the wildflowers already stood there.
So did the deed,
passed from a tavern keeper's widow to a man with a plan.
The first taking had set the pattern.
Whoever held the paper would claim this ground, clear it, and remake it,
again and again.
